lead: A group homomorphism is a function between groups that respects the operation: f(ab)=f(a)f(b). Its kernel collects the elements sent to the identity. Kernels are always normal subgroups: for H=ker f, gHg⁻¹=H for every g ∈ G. So the cosets of the kernel form a quotient group. The first isomorphism theorem says the quotient by the kernel is isomorphic to the image. This idea is used to compare groups, prove non-isomorphism, and reduce questions about a group to smaller quotient groups.
prereq: You need: groups and subgroups from 4.2, cosets and Lagrange from 4.4, and functions from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Let G and G′ be groups, with identities e and e′. A group homomorphism is a function f: G → G′ such that f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for all a,b in G. Here ab is the product in G, while f(a)f(b) is the product in G′. The order of the factors matters: in a non-abelian group ab and ba can be different. Two consequences follow from the definition. First, f(e)=e′: apply f to ee=e and cancel f(e). Second, f(a⁻¹)=f(a)⁻¹: apply f to aa⁻¹=e. These are not extra axioms; they are derived. The kernel is ker f = {g ∈ G : f(g)=e′}. The image is im f = {f(g) : g ∈ G}. The kernel measures what f collapses to the identity; the image is the part of G′ actually reached. A bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism. Isomorphic groups have the same group-theoretic structure.

Fix a subgroup H of G. H is normal if gHg⁻¹=H for every g ∈ G, where gHg⁻¹ = {ghg⁻¹ : h ∈ H}. Equivalently, gH=Hg for every g: left cosets and right cosets agree as sets. The kernel of any homomorphism f: G→G′ is normal. Proof: take k ∈ ker f and g ∈ G. Then f(gkg⁻¹)=f(g)f(k)f(g⁻¹)=f(g)e′f(g)⁻¹=e′, so gkg⁻¹ ∈ ker f. Thus g(ker f)g⁻¹ ⊆ ker f; replacing g by g⁻¹ gives equality. When H is normal, the set G/H of cosets becomes a group under (aH)(bH)=abH. The identity is H, and the inverse of aH is a⁻¹H. Well-definedness needs normality: if aH=a′H and bH=b′H, then a′b′H=abH. The group G/H is the quotient group. When G is additive, such as Z, we write cosets as r+6Z and the operation as (r+6Z)+(s+6Z)=(r+s)+6Z; this is the same coset construction as aH above. Its order is [G:H], the index of H, and |G|=|H|[G:H] when G is finite.

First isomorphism theorem. Let f: G→G′ be a homomorphism. Then G/ker f ≅ im f. The isomorphism is φ: G/ker f → im f, φ(g ker f)=f(g). It is well-defined because if g ker f = g′ ker f, then g′⁻¹g ∈ ker f, so f(g′)=f(g). It is a homomorphism because φ((a ker f)(b ker f))=φ(ab ker f)=f(ab)=f(a)f(b). It is injective: φ(g ker f)=e′ means g ∈ ker f, so g ker f = ker f. It is surjective onto im f by definition. Example 1: f: Z→Zₙ, f(m)=m mod n. The kernel is nZ={…,−n,0,n,2n,…}; the image is Zₙ; so Z/nZ ≅ Zₙ. Example 2: the sign map sgn: Sₙ→{1,−1} for n≥2. Here Sₙ is the group of all permutations of n symbols under composition, and sign(σ)=+1 for even permutations and −1 for odd permutations. It is a homomorphism because sign(στ)=sign(σ)sign(τ). The kernel is the alternating group Aₙ, and Sₙ/Aₙ ≅ {1,−1}. The quotient has two cosets, Aₙ and the odd permutations.
Only a few syllabi add rings and fields at this point. Their definitions belong to the rings-and-fields chapter, not this one.

figure.caption: The kernel 6Z collapses to the identity, and the quotient Z/6Z matches the image Z₆.

spec.title: First isomorphism theorem for f(n)=n mod 6
spec.aria: A map f from Z to Z6 has kernel 6Z, and the quotient Z/6Z is isomorphic to the image Z6.

examples.question: Let f: Z → Z₆ be f(n)=n mod 6. (a) Find ker f. (b) Find im f. (c) Verify the first isomorphism theorem by giving an isomorphism Z/ker f → im f. (d) State |im f| and [Z:6Z].
steps: f(n)=0 in Z₆ exactly when n≡0 mod 6. So ker f = {6k : k∈Z} = 6Z = {…,−12,−6,0,6,12,…}.
The residues modulo 6 are 0,1,2,3,4,5. So im f = {0,1,2,3,4,5} = Z₆, which has 6 elements.
The quotient Z/6Z has the six cosets r+6Z for r=0,1,2,3,4,5.
Define φ: Z/6Z → Z₆ by φ(r+6Z)=r mod 6. If r+6Z=s+6Z, then r−s=6k, so r≡s mod 6; φ is well-defined.
φ is a homomorphism: φ((r+6Z)+(s+6Z))=φ((r+s)+6Z)=(r+s) mod 6=(r mod 6)+(s mod 6) in Z₆.
The six cosets map to the six residues 0,1,2,3,4,5. Thus φ is injective and surjective, hence an isomorphism Z/6Z ≅ Z₆.
examples.answer: ker f = 6Z, im f = Z₆, and the map r+6Z ↦ r mod 6 is an isomorphism Z/6Z → Z₆; |im f| = 6 and [Z:6Z] = 6.
examples.check:
n = 6
image_size = len({m % n for m in range(n)})
cosets = {m % n for m in range(n)}
print(image_size)
print(len(cosets))

traps: Thinking every subgroup is normal. The kernel of a homomorphism is always normal, but an arbitrary subgroup need not be. Test gHg⁻¹=H.
Treating f(e)=e′ and f(a⁻¹)=f(a)⁻¹ as extra axioms. They follow from f(ab)=f(a)f(b); still check them in calculations.
Writing G/H as a group without checking that H is normal. For a non-normal subgroup, coset multiplication may depend on representatives.
Confusing G with G/ker f. The first isomorphism theorem gives G/ker f ≅ im f, not G ≅ im f in general.
For the sign map Sₙ→{1,−1}, saying the kernel is {1}. The kernel is the alternating group Aₙ; the quotient has order 2.

quiz.q: Define a group homomorphism f: G → G′.
quiz.a: A function f: G → G′ such that f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for all a,b ∈ G. The product ab is in G and f(a)f(b) is in G′.

quiz.q: Define a normal subgroup H of a group G.
quiz.a: H is a subgroup of G (written H ≤ G) and is normal if gHg⁻¹=H for every g ∈ G, equivalently gH=Hg for every g ∈ G.

quiz.q: Why is the kernel of a homomorphism f: G → G′ a normal subgroup?
quiz.a: For k ∈ ker f and g ∈ G, f(gkg⁻¹)=f(g)f(k)f(g⁻¹)=f(g)e′f(g)⁻¹=e′. So gkg⁻¹ ∈ ker f. This gives g(ker f)g⁻¹ ⊆ ker f; replacing g by g⁻¹ gives equality.

quiz.q: Let f: Z → Z₄ be f(n)=n mod 4. Find ker f, im f, and the order of Z/ker f.
quiz.a: ker f = 4Z = {…,−4,0,4,8,…}. im f = Z₄ = {0,1,2,3}. Z/4Z has 4 cosets, so its order is 4.

quiz.q: For n≥2, the sign map sgn: Sₙ → {1,−1} is a homomorphism. State its kernel and the order of Sₙ/ker(sgn).
quiz.a: The kernel is the alternating group Aₙ, the even permutations. The quotient Sₙ/Aₙ has order 2. (Sₙ is the group of all permutations of n symbols under composition; sign(σ)=+1 for even permutations and −1 for odd permutations.)

quiz.q: If H is a subgroup of G of index 2, show that H is normal.
quiz.a: There are exactly two left cosets: H and G\H, where G\H means the set of elements of G not in H. There are exactly two right cosets: H and G\H. If g∈H, then gH=H=Hg. If g∉H, then gH=G\H=Hg. So gH=Hg for every g, hence H is normal.

quiz.q: Let f: G → G′ be a homomorphism. Prove that f is injective if and only if ker f = {e}.
quiz.a: If f is injective, f(g)=e′=f(e) implies g=e, so ker f={e}. Conversely, if ker f={e} and f(a)=f(b), then f(ab⁻¹)=f(a)f(b)⁻¹=e′, so ab⁻¹=e, hence a=b. Thus f is injective.

beyond: Not for the exam. Normal subgroups and quotient groups are the language of symmetry breaking in physics and of error-correcting codes built from groups. In computer science, quotient constructions appear in automata minimization and in type theory. Ring theory leads to finite fields, which underpin AES and Reed-Solomon codes. Search terms: quotient group, first isomorphism theorem, finite field GF(2⁸) (the field with 256 elements), group action.
